html:
Friday, March 14, 2014. Sunny.


Reviewer: myself, 1,835 days later.

Date of review: Sunday, March 23, 2019. Sunny.


Preface: As it happens, I’m typing this entry up for Zhihu just after getting back from this same conference, D. It was my fifth time at D, five years after the first. Every conference feels different, and this was the first time I attended not as a student, which stirred up a lot of feelings.

Back from the conference!

I was basically just along for the ride the whole time, and the German Vorträge, the talks, gave me a splitting headache every day. I didn’t really meet anyone or talk to anyone, and didn’t get a lot out of it. I did chat with MK for a while, but nothing of substance. I feel that when you don’t have much in your head, you don’t have much to bring to a conversation. I think next year will be better. One step at a time! Lately I’m no longer as anxious about everything as I used to be, which is a good thing. On the other hand, I need to push harder; this mustn’t become the start of slacking off. Staying productive with nobody supervising you and no concrete tasks is incredibly hard! Find the right way to motivate yourself! *

Reviewer’s comments: Many years later, the author has finally found a way to motivate himself: leaving academia XD. This was his first academic conference, and he landed in one armed to the teeth with German. Unfortunately for him, German acoustics is so damn good that the Germans can run the whole show in their own language and get away with it. Over three days his mood went from excitement on the first day to dejection on the last, a very obvious swing, because he couldn’t understand a bloody word! He had passed A1 German, but that was no damn use at all. Apart from the figures and the words that looked like English, he sat there like an idiot. On the last day a colleague asked him, how was your first conference? His answer was pretty blunt: Terrible. This time he went as an exhibitor with his company. There I met a PhD student who was on exchange at my old German institute. The moment he saw me he gave me a pained smile and said he couldn’t understand a thing. Meals with his colleagues were awkward too: he couldn’t follow anything, and the Germans just ignored him. I know that feeling all too well. His description took me straight back to this conference trip five years ago.

The only thing I got out of it this time was learning that our institute is that damn good, one of the leaders in the field. No wonder my colleagues are so impressive.

Reviewer’s comments: Well, not completely true. Blame it on the author being such a noob back then that everyone looked awesome to him. At the time, a German in the group complained about me to a new colleague, saying I was slow, and then added: you know, Chinese. And him now? He presented the same stuff at D three years running, with almost no results, and he still hasn’t graduated in his sixth year. Looks like he’ll be leaving without a degree. Our institute and our boss really were that good, though. Later, when I was looking for a postdoc and when I moved into industry, I rode my PhD supervisor’s coattails, and they were sturdy ones.

As long as I don’t drag the institute down and can actually produce something myself, I’ll be satisfied!

Reviewer’s comments: Looking back, I didn’t drag anyone down. In fact I published more papers than most of the institute’s PhD graduates, haha. Although I was low for a while after this conference, it really did open my eyes: it was the first time I came into contact with researchers from elsewhere in the field. What really made me realize how important conferences are was an international conference two years later. I met a lot of people there, and by then I had some results to show and talk about. It was also at that conference that I apologized to the professor who would later be my postdoc boss (because I had turned down his offer earlier), and met the CTO of my current company. Many people think conferences are a waste of time and conference papers aren’t worth much. I agree completely with the second half and disagree completely with the first. For building a network, broadening your horizons and advancing your career, conferences matter far, far more than the much-vaunted papers in SCI-indexed journals. I always encourage the PhD students around me to seize every chance to go to conferences, even if their work is crap, even if the conference isn’t in a tourist city.
